mcqs.question: Why should a user's balance be derived from expense and settlement history rather than stored as an independently-updated number?
options: Because storing a derived value is always faster to query than history
Because databases cannot store a running total field
Because a bug or missed update to a standalone counter permanently corrupts the ledger, while derived balances can always be recomputed and reconciled against the underlying events
Because Splitwise groups are limited to a fixed number of members
mcqs.explanation: Treating expenses/settlements as the source of truth means the balance can always be verified or rebuilt by replaying history, so a bug is recoverable rather than a silent permanent error. Databases can absolutely store running totals (and this design still does, as a materialized view) — the point is what's authoritative, not raw query speed or membership limits.

mcqs.question: Splitting 1001 cents equally three ways using integer division and remainder assignment gives which result?
options: 333, 333, 333 — with 2 cents silently lost to rounding
333.67, 333.67, 333.67 stored as floating point
It fails validation because 1001 doesn't divide evenly by 3
334, 334, 333 — the first two participants (by stable order) each get one extra cent
mcqs.explanation: base = 1001/3 = 333, remainder = 1001%3 = 2, so the first two participants get 334 and the last gets 333 — summing to exactly 1001. Nothing is lost to rounding, no floating point is used, and an uneven division is expected, not an error.

mcqs.question: Why is debt simplification necessary even though every expense already produces correct per-participant splits?
options: Because settling with one payment per original expense could mean dozens of small transfers, when the group's actual net positions could be settled with far fewer payments
Because splits are frequently miscalculated and need to be corrected before settling
Because expenses older than 30 days must be deleted before settle-up
Because Split objects cannot be summed across multiple expenses
mcqs.explanation: Splits are correct as computed; the problem is that many small pairwise debts are redundant once netted — simplification collapses them into a minimal set of payments using each person's net position, not because anything upstream was wrong. There's no expense expiry rule and Split objects sum fine across expenses.

mcqs.question: In the greedy two-heap debt-simplification algorithm, why does matching the largest creditor with the largest debtor each round guarantee at most n-1 transactions for n people?
options: Because it always finds the theoretical global minimum number of transactions
Because each round settles the smaller of the two matched amounts, which fully zeroes out at least one person (creditor or debtor) every round
Because the algorithm stops after exactly n-1 rounds regardless of remaining balances
Because only the two largest balances in the entire group are ever allowed to settle
mcqs.explanation: Settling min(c.amount, d.amount) each round drives at least one side to exactly zero, removing that person from further rounds — with n people, at most n-1 removals are needed before at most one remains. This greedy approach isn't proven globally minimal in every case (that's a harder, NP-hard problem in general), and it doesn't restrict matching to only the two largest balances overall — it re-picks the current largest each round.

mcqs.question: Why does the debt-simplification algorithm operate on net balances per user rather than pairwise balances per user pair?
options: Pairwise balances are illegal to store under financial regulations
Pairwise balances cannot be computed from Split records
Net balances are exactly the algorithm's required input and match what a settle-up screen wants to show; pairwise data would need netting first anyway
Net balances take less storage than any other representation
mcqs.explanation: The simplification algorithm needs one net number per person, which is what net balances directly provide; pairwise balances are still useful for audit trails but would have to be netted down before the algorithm could use them. There's no regulatory bar on pairwise storage, and pairwise data is easy to compute from Splits — the issue is fitness for the algorithm, not legality or storage size.

mcqs.question: Two expenses affecting Alice's balance are added by different group members at nearly the same time. What prevents one update from silently overwriting the other?
options: Locking the entire group so only one member can add an expense at a time
Adding a 5-second delay between expense submissions
Recomputing Alice's balance from scratch once per day to catch any drift
Applying each balance change as an atomic increment (UPDATE ... SET amount = amount + ?) instead of a separate read-modify-write in application code
mcqs.explanation: An atomic increment has no separate read step that can go stale, so two concurrent updates both apply correctly regardless of ordering. Locking the whole group, adding artificial delays, or a daily recompute are heavier-handed or delayed fixes that don't address the actual race at write time.
